input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Both membranes were tested on one feed, 85 wt% ethanol in water at 60 °C; one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.4 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180, and its flux fell 10% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 560, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The two membranes divide the performance figures between them. The polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area and per hour; the zeolite membrane separates more sharply, with a permeate far richer in water, relative to alcohol, than the feed. Stability divides them in the same direction as selectivity: the polymer membrane loses flux over the test period, and the zeolite membrane holds its flux within measurement error. No ranking of the two membranes follows from these figures alone, because a duty sets the flux and the separation factor it requires, and neither requirement is stated here. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; here all three stand on the one feed composition, and behaviour at any other composition was not measured.
